planting.note: Set rooted divisions out after the last frost once soil has warmed; avoid rich or soggy ground.

directions: This is the smallest-leaved thyme in general cultivation, forming an almost moss-like, dense green mat only an inch or two tall. Tiny lilac-pink flowers cover the foliage in clusters during summer, drawing bees. It spreads slowly compared to other creeping thymes, so give it excellent drainage and lean soil rather than fertile beds. Shear lightly after bloom to keep the mat tight and encourage fresh growth.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in gritty, well-drained soil; avoid winter wet.

directions: Golden King forms low mounding clumps of lemon-scented leaves edged in bright gold against green centers, giving a two-tone variegated effect distinct from solid-gold lemon thyme forms. Pale lavender-pink flowers appear in spring and summer and are attractive to bees. It holds its color best in full sun and resents heavy or waterlogged soil over winter. Trim lightly after flowering to keep the clump compact and encourage new variegated growth.
sources: Ball Seed / Darwin Perennials plant info

planting.note: Divide and transplant in spring into lean, well-drained soil; do not over-fertilize.

directions: This white-flowered form of wild thyme forms a dense, low mat of small aromatic leaves topped with masses of pure white blooms in late spring to summer, a clean contrast to the more common pink and purple creeping thymes. Bees and other pollinators work the flowers heavily. It tolerates light foot traffic and releases fragrance when brushed or stepped on, making it well suited to paths and paver joints. Cut back after flowering to keep growth fresh and prevent woody, bare centers.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun; gold color is strongest with lean, dry soil.

directions: Aureus is grown mainly for its foliage, carrying tiny golden-yellow leaves on a creeping, mat-forming habit rather than for standout flowers, though small summer blooms do appear and draw bees. The gold coloring intensifies in full sun and fades toward green in shade, so siting matters. It tolerates heat, drought, and light foot traffic once established, making it a popular edging for paths and rock gardens. Shear lightly in late winter to remove tired growth and keep the color fresh.

planting.note: Set divisions or plugs in spring in sharply drained soil; keep off wet winter ground.

directions: Unlike standard woolly thyme, which rarely flowers, Hall's Woolly blooms profusely, covering its soft gray-green, fuzzy foliage with small lavender-pink flowers in summer. The dense, low wool-textured mat spreads widely and tolerates light foot traffic, making it a durable choice between stepping stones. It needs very sharp drainage and resents wet winters, so raised or sloped sites suit it best. Deer generally leave it alone, and pollinators visit readily when it is in bloom.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil; cut back in late winter to refresh growth.

directions: Pink Ripple takes its name from the dense waves of tiny pink flowers that wash over its semi-evergreen mat through summer, drawing bees and butterflies. The fine aromatic foliage stays low and tight, forming a durable carpet between pavers or over rocks. It needs cutting back at the end of winter to clear out old growth and keep the mat looking fresh for the coming season. Like other creeping thymes it demands sharp drainage and struggles in heavy or constantly damp soil.
